title: Broken Faith: The Priests, and the Wife of Your Youth
summary: God pronounces a curse on the priests who will not honor his name, contrasting them with Levi, who revered God, taught the truth, and turned many from sin. Then Malachi turns to the people: they break faith with one another by marrying women who worship foreign gods and by divorcing the wives of their youth, and they weary God by saying that he rewards evildoers or does not care about justice.
story: Chapter 1 exposed the priests' contempt at the altar. Chapter 2 finishes that case with a sentence and then widens the charge to the whole community. The link is the idea of covenant, which runs through the chapter: God's covenant with Levi, the covenant of the fathers that binds Israel together, and the covenant of marriage that God himself witnesses. The priests have failed to teach faithfully, and the people have learned from them to treat every commitment lightly. The chapter ends with a complaint, where is the God of justice, that sets up the answer of chapter 3: the Lord they seek is coming.
historical:
The problems here match what Ezra and Nehemiah found in Judah in the mid-fifth century BC. Ezra 9 and 10 describe returned exiles, including priests and Levites, who had married women from the surrounding peoples, and Nehemiah 13:23-29 records the same problem a generation later, along with a grandson of the high priest married into the family of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. The concern in those books and in Malachi was not ethnicity as such but worship: these marriages brought the gods of other peoples into Israelite homes, the very thing the prophets said had led to exile.

Verses 14 to 16 suggest that some men were divorcing their Israelite wives, perhaps to marry into wealthier or more influential families of the land. In a small, poor province, such marriages could bring land, trade, and status. For the abandoned wife the result could be poverty and disgrace.
cultural:
The priests of Israel came from the tribe of Levi, and their duties went beyond sacrifice. They were responsible for teaching the law (Deuteronomy 33:10; Leviticus 10:11) and for judging disputes, so that people went to the priest to learn what God required. The covenant with Levi in verses 4 to 6 recalls both Moses' blessing of Levi and the covenant of peace given to the priest Phinehas for his zeal (Numbers 25:12-13). The threat in verse 3 is shocking on purpose: the dung of sacrificial animals was carried outside the camp and burned (Exodus 29:14), and the priests who handled holy things would be treated as refuse.

Marriage in Israel was a legal and family arrangement, but the Old Testament also calls it a covenant (Proverbs 2:17; Ezekiel 16:8). Divorce was permitted under Deuteronomy 24:1-4, which required a written certificate that protected the woman's freedom to remarry. The wife of your youth in verses 14 and 15 is a tender phrase for a first wife married when both were young, and Malachi presents the man who discards her as betraying a companion and a covenant partner, with God himself as witness to the vows.
literary: The chapter completes the second disputation (1:6 to 2:9) and contains the third (2:10-16) and the opening of the fourth (2:17, which continues into 3:5). The priestly section is framed by the contrast between what Levi was (verses 5 to 7) and what his descendants have become (verses 8 and 9), with the word covenant repeated at its turning points. The third disputation opens with rhetorical questions (Do we not all have one Father?) and is held together by the verb break faith, used five times in verses 10 to 16. The Hebrew of verses 15 and 16 is among the most difficult in the prophets, and translations differ considerably there.

outline.t: A curse on priests who will not honor God's name
The covenant with Levi: what a priest should be
Priests who cause many to stumble
Judah profanes the covenant by marrying foreign worshipers
Tears at the altar and the wife of your youth
Wearying God: where is the God of justice?

doctrines.note: Covenant links worship and ethics in this chapter. The same people who break faith with God break faith with one another, and God treats both as a single betrayal of the covenant of the fathers.
Marriage is a covenant God witnesses. Malachi treats the discarding of a faithful wife as a wrong God sees and hates, and connects faithful marriage with the raising of godly children.
The priest was the LORD's messenger, entrusted with true instruction. When teachers of God's word bend it through partiality, they cause many to stumble, and God holds them accountable.

words.note: Berit, covenant. It appears five times here: the covenant with Levi (verses 4, 5, and 8), the covenant of the fathers (verse 10), and the wife by covenant (verse 14). A covenant was a binding relationship sealed by oath, and Malachi uses the word to show that every bond in Israel's life, with God and with one another, rests on faithfulness.

Torah, instruction or law. Its root sense is teaching, direction for how to live, and here it names what should come from the priest's mouth (verses 6 to 9). The word later names the five books of Moses, but in this chapter it refers to the living teaching the priests were meant to give.

Shalach, to send away, here used in the sense of divorce in verse 16. The same verb elsewhere means simply to send. Deuteronomy 24:1 uses it of sending a wife away with a certificate. How to translate the verse that contains it is disputed, as the hard question below explains.

Echad, one. The chapter's argument pivots on it: one Father, one God who created us (verse 10), and the LORD who made husband and wife one (verse 15, echoing Genesis 2:24). Unity with God grounds faithfulness to one another.

christ: Malachi's picture of the faithful priest, with true instruction in his mouth, walking with God in peace and uprightness and turning many from iniquity (verses 6 and 7), describes what Israel's priests were meant to be and so often were not. The New Testament presents Jesus as the priest who fulfills that calling perfectly: Hebrews describes him as a high priest who is holy, innocent, and undefiled (Hebrews 7:26), and Matthew closes the Sermon on the Mount by noting that he taught with authority, not as the scribes (Matthew 7:28-29). On marriage, Jesus goes back to the same creation text Malachi alludes to, that the two become one flesh, and answers a question about divorce by insisting on the permanence God intended (Matthew 19:3-9). Paul later describes marriage as a picture of the covenant between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25-32), and that is the deepest reason Malachi can call a husband's faithlessness a betrayal of God's covenant.

hard.q: Does God really say I hate divorce, and what does that mean for people who have been divorced?
hard.a:
The Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult. Read literally it says something like for he hates, sending away, and the subject of hate is unclear. The BSB and many older translations take God as the subject: God hates divorce. Several recent translations take the husband as the subject, rendering it along the lines of the man who hates and divorces his wife covers his garment with violence (the NIV of 2011 and the ESV take roughly this approach). The ancient versions also differ. On either reading the verse condemns a man who callously discards a faithful wife, and it calls that act violence.

The passage is aimed at men who were breaking covenant, not at those who were abandoned or wronged. Scripture permits divorce in some cases (Deuteronomy 24:1-4; Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15), and Christians differ on exactly which. What Malachi makes plain is that God sees the harm done when marriage vows are broken and takes the side of the one betrayed.

questions: Malachi says a priest's lips should preserve knowledge. What makes a teacher of Scripture trustworthy, and how should teachers be held accountable?
Verse 10 ties faithfulness to God to faithfulness to one another. Where do you see those two go together, or come apart, in your own life?
The people weary God by saying he doesn't care about justice. How do you respond when it looks as if evildoers prosper?
